body:
What is science policy?

Science policy refers to the principles and decisions through which a government promotes scientific research, develops technological capabilities and encourages the use of knowledge for national development. It helps determine which areas need research support, how scientific institutions should cooperate and how discoveries can benefit society.

Scientific research requires trained people, laboratories, equipment, funding and time. Some research produces immediate benefits, while other investigations improve fundamental knowledge that may become useful much later. A national science policy must therefore support both scientific excellence and practical public needs.

Science, technology and innovation

Although these terms are closely related, they have different meanings.

  • Science: Systematic investigation of natural phenomena through observation, evidence, experimentation and reasoning. For example, studying how microorganisms cause disease produces scientific knowledge.
  • Technology: The application of knowledge to develop useful methods, processes, instruments or products. A diagnostic test that detects a microorganism is an example of technology.
  • Innovation: The development and successful use of a new or significantly improved solution. Making a reliable diagnostic test affordable and accessible to rural health centres illustrates innovation.

A scientific discovery does not automatically become an innovation. A useful solution must be developed, tested for its intended purpose and made available to users. Innovation can also improve an existing product or service rather than create something entirely new.

Research and development (R&D) includes systematic work that generates new knowledge and uses knowledge to create or improve products, processes and services. Basic research seeks greater understanding; applied research addresses a defined practical problem.

How research reaches society

A university may identify a scientific principle. A research laboratory may use it to develop a technology. An industry, public institution or government programme may then make that technology available to people. These activities often overlap, but their roles are not identical.

For example, agricultural researchers may develop a crop variety that tolerates water stress. Agricultural universities and field institutions can assess its performance under local conditions. Extension workers can then explain its appropriate use to farmers. The resulting benefit depends not only on discovery but also on testing, communication, affordability and adoption.

Evolution of India's national science policies

Independent India developed successive policies as its scientific capabilities and development needs changed.

YearPolicyPrincipal emphasis
1958Scientific Policy ResolutionBuilding scientific research capacity and promoting science.
1983Technology Policy StatementTechnological competence and self-reliance.
2003Science and Technology PolicyStronger integration of science, technology and national development.
2013Science, Technology and Innovation PolicyConnecting research with innovation and inclusive growth.
2020Draft Science, Technology and Innovation PolicyProposed reforms in open science, research financing and participation.

The movement from science to technology and then to innovation does not mean that basic science became unimportant. Rather, each successive framework placed additional emphasis on connecting knowledge with national needs.

Scientific temper and public participation

Scientific temper means approaching claims with curiosity, reason and evidence instead of accepting them merely because they are customary or widely repeated. Article 51A(h) of the Constitution places the development of scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform among the Fundamental Duties of citizens.

Scientific literacy helps people make informed decisions about health, agriculture, environmental protection and technology. Science policy therefore concerns education and public awareness as well as research laboratories.

Prelims focus

  • 1958: Scientific Policy Resolution.
  • 1983: Technology Policy Statement.
  • 2003: Science and Technology Policy.
  • 2013: Science, Technology and Innovation Policy.
  • 2020: Draft of the proposed 5th national STI policy.
  • Article 51A(h) concerns scientific temper, humanism, inquiry and reform.
  • Trap: A policy proposal is not necessarily an enacted law or an implemented programme.

[Government of India, Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013, sections Changing Phases of National Policies in S&T and The Need for a Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, pp. 1–2; Department of Science and Technology, Draft STIP, December 2020, section Evolution of STI Policies in India; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Article 51A(h); sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Science Policy in India: Meaning, Purpose and Evolution

body:
Why was the 2013 policy introduced?

India had already developed research institutions, scientific manpower and important technologies. The central challenge was to connect this capacity more effectively with economic development and social needs. The Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013 therefore emphasised that scientific progress should contribute to both economic prosperity and public welfare.

Its guiding approach was science, technology and innovation for the people. Research could be internationally competitive while also addressing problems involving food, water, healthcare, energy, the environment and employment.

Principal objectives

  • Scientific temper: Encourage inquiry, scientific understanding and the application of evidence in everyday life.
  • Human resources: Attract talented students to scientific careers and strengthen research skills.
  • Research infrastructure: Improve laboratories, equipment and facilities needed for high-quality investigation.
  • Scientific excellence: Increase India's ability to undertake internationally competitive research.
  • Inclusive development: Promote solutions that are accessible and affordable to a broad section of society.
  • Industry participation: Encourage private investment, partnerships and the practical use of research findings.
  • Innovation: Help discoveries become useful products, processes and public services.

The policy did not treat excellence and social relevance as competing goals. Strong scientific research can produce new knowledge, while collaboration with users can help determine where that knowledge is needed.

Important quantitative aspirations

The 2013 policy identified several ambitious national targets. These must be read as policy goals stated in 2013, not as proof that the targets were subsequently achieved.

Indicator2013 policy statementCorrect interpretation
Research expenditureRaise GERD to 2% of GDP.A national expenditure target.
Private participationIncrease private R&D investment to at least match public investment.An intended change in funding contributions.
Scientific standingPosition India among the top 5 global scientific powers by 2020.A time-bound aspiration.
Research workforceIncrease full-time-equivalent R&D personnel by at least 66% over the following 5 years.A proposed expansion in research capacity.

What does GERD measure?

Gross Expenditure on Research and Development (GERD) measures total domestic expenditure on R&D during a specified period. Expressing GERD as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) indicates how much of the economy's output is devoted to research.

The policy described India's R&D expenditure at that time as below 1% of GDP and the private-to-public investment ratio as approximately 1:3. It proposed increasing private investment so that private and public contributions would at least become equal. The 1:3 ratio is therefore a historical baseline mentioned in the policy, not a permanently valid ratio.

A target such as 2% of GDP or a top-5 ranking is not an achieved statistical result merely because it appears in a government policy. The year, baseline and intended outcome must remain attached to the statement.

Research partnerships and inclusive innovation

Government-funded research often creates knowledge and public benefits that private firms may not initially find profitable. Industry can contribute technical development, production capacity and market access. The 2013 policy sought to strengthen public-private partnerships (PPPs) so that research could move more effectively towards practical use.

For example, scientists may identify a low-cost method for treating contaminated water. A research institution can assess its effectiveness, an enterprise can produce suitable equipment and a public agency can help introduce it in underserved communities. The public benefit depends on coordination across these stages.

The policy also emphasised research in universities, opportunities for women scientists, access to shared scientific facilities and stronger links between national research and state-level development priorities.

Prelims focus

  • STI Policy 2013 linked scientific excellence with inclusive economic growth.
  • GERD target: 2% of GDP.
  • Historical private-to-public R&D investment ratio cited by the policy: approximately 1:3.
  • Proposed direction: private R&D investment should at least match public investment.
  • The top-5 scientific-powers-by-2020 statement was an aspiration.
  • Trap: GERD is expenditure on research and development, not total government expenditure on education.

[Government of India, Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013, sections STI Policy: A New Paradigm, Capturing Aspirations, Investment in Research and Development, Promoting Excellence and Relevance in R&D, and Attracting Private Sector Investments in R&D, pp. 2–11; Department of Science and Technology, official policy document, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A water-treatment discovery becomes affordable clean-water treatment through research assessment, industry production and public-agency support for access.
pictures.caption: Inclusive innovation requires more than a scientific discovery.

title: Science, Technology and Innovation Policy 2013: Objectives and Targets

body:
What was the 2020 initiative?

The Government of India began preparing a new Science, Technology and Innovation Policy (STIP) during 2020. It was described as the proposed 5th national science and technology policy. The Department of Science and Technology and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser organised consultations intended to obtain views from researchers, institutions, industries and the public.

The December 2020 document was issued as a draft for consultation. It set out proposed reforms rather than an automatically enforceable set of government measures.

In an official statement dated 29 January 2026, the Government of India explicitly stated that the national STIP 2020 was only a draft document and that no budget allocation or expenditure was made under it. Later research initiatives must therefore be identified through their own approvals, laws or schemes rather than being attributed automatically to implementation of the entire draft.

How did the proposed approach differ?

The draft sought a more decentralised, evidence-driven, inclusive and participatory research system. A decentralised approach allows priorities and ideas to emerge from institutions and communities rather than only from central authorities. Evidence-driven planning uses information about research needs, resources and outcomes to guide decisions.

Major themes included open science, research financing, stronger universities, inclusion, science communication, entrepreneurship and the domestic development of technologies.

Open science and research access

Open science aims to make scientific knowledge, research outputs and suitable facilities more accessible so that researchers and the public can use them. Access must still respect privacy, national security, intellectual property and other legitimate restrictions.

The draft proposed several mechanisms:

  • National STI Observatory: A proposed information system for collecting and examining data about research programmes, funding, institutions and results.
  • Indian Science and Technology Archive of Research (INDSTA): A proposed platform for accessing outputs of publicly funded research.
  • Open research data: Wider access to suitable research information using FAIR principles.
  • One Nation, One Subscription: A proposal for centrally negotiated access to scholarly journals.
  • Shared scientific resources: Better access to publicly funded research equipment, facilities and educational resources.

FAIR principles

The abbreviation FAIR describes research data that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. Interoperability means that data can be understood or exchanged between suitable systems. Reusability means that others can use the data appropriately, with the necessary information and conditions.

FAIR does not mean that every dataset must be released without restrictions. Personal medical information, security-sensitive findings and protected intellectual property may require controlled access or other safeguards.

Draft proposals versus actual programmes

A government may later introduce a separate scheme resembling an earlier policy proposal. Such a scheme must be assessed according to its own official notification and implementation arrangements. The existence of a similar programme does not establish that all provisions of the draft STIP 2020 became operative.

AspectSTI Policy 2013Draft STIP 2020
Document statusNational policy issued in 2013.Consultation draft issued in 2020.
Major emphasisResearch excellence, investment and inclusive innovation.Open science, participation, financing and research-system reform.
Research informationBetter measures of research and innovation outcomes.Proposed National STI Observatory and INDSTA.
InterpretationRead its goals as policy aspirations.Read its provisions as proposals unless separately implemented.

Prelims focus

  • STIP 2020 was prepared as the proposed 5th national STI policy.
  • The publicly released draft was dated December 2020.
  • INDSTA was proposed for access to publicly funded research outputs.
  • FAIR means Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable.
  • The National STI Observatory was a proposed research-information mechanism.
  • On 29 January 2026, the Government confirmed that STIP 2020 had been only a draft.
  • Trap: A proposal for a programme does not prove that the programme was implemented through the draft policy.

[Department of Science and Technology, Draft Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, December 2020, version 1.4, Executive Summary and Chapter 1: Open Science, especially sections 1.1–1.5; DST, Consultation Process for New Science, Technology and Innovation Policy; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Science and Technology, Implementation of National Science, Technology and Innovation Policy-2020, 29 January 2026; sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
